content: 1. There is no evidence of sustained human-to-human transmission of avian influenza A, nor is there evidence to suggest airborne transmission between humans. Therefore, a medical mask is sufficient for routine care. 2. Current evidence indicates that SARS transmission in healthcare settings primarily occurs through droplet and contact routes. Thus, a medical mask is adequate for routine care. 3. Certain aerosol-generating procedures have been associated with an increased risk of transmission of SARS and tuberculosis. However, the infectious risk associated with aerosol-generating procedures in patients with bacterial acute respiratory diseases (ARDs), or ARDs caused by rhinovirus, parainfluenza, RSV, and adenovirus, remains undefined. At a minimum, a tightly-fitted medical mask should be used during such procedures. 4. Patients should cover their nose and mouth with tissues, handkerchiefs, or their hands when coughing or sneezing to prevent the spread of respiratory secretions. 5. Children, who may not be able to comply with these recommendations, are common carriers of respiratory pathogens. 6. Patients with the same diagnosis should be cohorted together. If this is not feasible, patient beds should be placed at least 1 meter apart. 7. Airborne precaution rooms should be ventilated either naturally or mechanically, with an air change rate of at least 12 air changes per hour (ACH) and controlled airflow direction. 8. Airborne precautions are necessary for diseases such as pulmonary tuberculosis, chickenpox, measles, and for novel organisms causing ARDs. 9. Healthcare facilities (HCFs) should establish or strengthen infection control committees and programs with trained personnel to ensure infection control policies are up-to-date and compliance is monitored. 10. Infection control measures should include infrastructure changes, education, posters, reminders, senior management engagement, and performance feedback. 11. Healthcare workers (HCWs) should be educated to follow infection control precautions for all patients with acute febrile respiratory illness. 12. Adequate supplies of protective equipment, such as closed protective footwear, waterproof aprons, and rubber gloves, as well as cleaning and disinfection materials, should be ensured. 13. Plans should be developed for the evaluation and management of patients suspected or confirmed to have ARDs of potential concern, including rapid screening, triage, and immediate implementation of infection control precautions. 14. Public health authorities should be promptly notified of any suspected or confirmed cases of ARDs of potential concern. 15. Signage should be posted at all entrances and clinical evaluation areas to alert patients and visitors to report severe acute febrile respiratory illness immediately to healthcare providers. 16. Once a patient with a confirmed ARD of potential concern is admitted, infection control surveillance should be increased to detect transmission to other patients and HCWs. 17. Hospital administrators and governments play a critical role in creating institutional conditions that promote the prevention of healthcare-associated pathogen spread. This includes written guidelines, adequate resources, promotion of adherence to infection control practices, and administrative leadership. 18. Lessons from the SARS outbreak highlight the importance of clear policies, management support for occupational health and safety, adequate training in infection control procedures, and access to specialists. 19. Infection control precautions for ARDs should be tailored based on epidemiological and clinical clues, suspected or confirmed causative agents, and the type of patient contact. 20. Aerosol-generating procedures have the potential to increase the risk of infection transmission, warranting enhanced personal protection during such procedures. 21. Cohorting involves placing patients infected or colonized with the same pathogens in the same designated unit. When single rooms are unavailable, cohorting should be implemented with spatial separation of at least 1 meter between patients. 22. Shared equipment should be avoided, but if unavoidable, reusable equipment must be disinfected appropriately between patients. 23. Regular cleaning and disinfection of common areas, as well as proper hand hygiene by patients, visitors, and caregivers, are essential. 24. For ARDs of potential concern, if single isolation rooms are insufficient, cohorting or special measures should be applied. HCWs assigned to these patients should be experienced and not float to other care areas. 25. The number of persons entering isolation or cohorting areas should be limited to the minimum necessary for patient care and support. 26. Portable X-ray equipment should be designated for use in assigned areas. 27. ARD patients should wear medical masks during transport to contain respiratory droplets. Surfaces contacted by patients should be cleaned and disinfected afterward. 28. HCWs transporting ARD patients should wear appropriate personal protective equipment (PPE) and perform hand hygiene afterward. 29. Pre-hospital care and transport of ARD patients should include screening for risk factors, avoiding aerosol-generating procedures, and notifying the receiving facility in advance. 30. Infection control precautions should be implemented based on the known or presumed infectious period of the specific ARD. 31. For avian and pandemic influenza, precautions should be age-specific: adults and adolescents (>12 years) require precautions for 7 days after symptom resolution, while infants and children (≤12 years) require precautions for 21 days after symptom onset. 32. Immunocompromised patients may shed pathogens for prolonged periods, and microbiologic monitoring is advised to determine the absence of detectable pathogens. 33. For SARS, infection control precautions should be maintained while patients are symptomatic. The duration of infectivity is not well-defined, but no SARS-CoV has been cultured from asymptomatic patients. 34. For newly emerging ARDs, precautions should continue until one week after symptom resolution or until laboratory evidence confirms no active infection. 35. Patients discharged during the infectious period should have their infection risk assessed, and infection control measures must be guaranteed in the home setting. 36. A verbal assessment of the patient’s home environment should be conducted before discharge to ensure it is suitable for safe home care. 37. Patients and caregivers should be instructed on proper hand hygiene, cough etiquette, and the use of PPE if necessary. 38. Vulnerable household members, such as those with chronic diseases, young children, or the elderly, should avoid contact with the patient until they are asymptomatic. 39. Visitors should be advised of the risk of ARD transmission and screened before entering the facility. 40. Visitors should use PPE as per HCF guidance and be instructed in its use and hand hygiene practices before entering isolation areas. 41. Family members and visitors with respiratory symptoms should be evaluated for infection and considered possible ARD cases. 42. The patient’s right to receive visits and the child’s right to be accompanied by a parent or legal guardian should be guaranteed, but infection control measures must be maintained.
